paragraphs.heading: The hump before the change
paragraphs.text: Activation energy is the smallest energy barrier that reacting molecules have to get over before they can turn into products. A reaction only happens when enough molecules have kinetic energy at least as large as this barrier, and that usually calls for a high enough temperature. The Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius coined the term in 1889. It is used less often outside chemistry, but the idea also applies to nuclear reactions and other physical processes.

paragraphs.heading: Reading it from temperature
paragraphs.text: In the Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(−Eₐ/RT), the symbol Eₐ is the activation energy needed to reach the transition state. Here k is the rate coefficient, A is the pre-exponential factor, R is the universal gas constant and T is the absolute temperature, usually in kelvins. Eₐ can be worked out from how k changes with temperature, even when A is unknown. At a deeper level, it is best seen as a measured number that shows how sensitive a reaction's rate is to temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Not quite a single barrier
paragraphs.text: There are two objections to treating this measured value as the height of one barrier in a single step. First, it is often unclear whether a reaction really happens in one step, and a barrier averaged over many steps tells theory little. Second, even a true one-step reaction measured in bulk involves billions of molecules. Their collisions come at many angles and energies, and each kind may react at its own rate.

paragraphs.heading: What a catalyst changes
paragraphs.text: A catalyst is a substance that lowers the activation energy by changing the transition state, and it speeds up a reaction without being used up. An enzyme is a catalyst made only of protein, sometimes with small molecules called cofactors. A catalyst leaves the energies of the starting reactants and of the final products as they were, so it does not shift the equilibrium. Only the barrier in between gets lower.

paragraphs.heading: Binding energy
paragraphs.text: A catalyst gives the substance being changed, called the substrate, a more comfortable fit on its way to the transition state. When the substrate settles into the catalyst's active site, stabilizing forces such as hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces act on it and release energy. That released energy is called binding energy, and it helps the substrate reach the unstable transition state. Reactions without a catalyst have no such energy to draw on, so they need a larger energy input.

paragraphs.heading: A second equation
paragraphs.text: Transition state theory, a more detailed model, describes the rate constant with the Eyring equation, k = (k_BT / h) exp(−ΔG^(‡) / RT), in which k_B stands for the Boltzmann constant and h for the Planck constant. In place of Eₐ it uses ΔG^(‡), the Gibbs energy of activation. The Arrhenius approach describes how rate depends on temperature as it is observed, while Eyring models the single elementary steps of a reaction. The two look alike, but the Gibbs energy carries an entropy term as well, which Arrhenius folds into A.

paragraphs.heading: A useful rule of thumb
paragraphs.text: For a one-step reaction of a single molecule with a half-life of about 2 hours at room temperature, ΔG^(‡) is roughly 23 kcal/mol. Eₐ is about the same size for a reaction that takes several hours at room temperature. Because the gaps between Eₐ, ΔG^(‡) and the enthalpy of activation ΔH^(‡) are small at ordinary temperatures, people loosely call all three the activation energy. Activation energy also says nothing about whether a reaction is spontaneous, and the total free energy change does not depend on it.
